A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLBiMan and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained material can be matched reliably despite added appendix sections and relocated displays.

before.justification: v1 reports original real-robot experiments on ten bimanual tasks, component ablations, lighting and interference tests, and cross-embodiment evaluations.

after.justification: v3 retains original robot experiments, revises the main quantitative results, and adds object-generalization, clutter, and interpolation-density evaluations.

M1.justification: The decomposition, vision-language anchoring, orientation estimation, IK refinement, and collision-compensation procedures remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the default interpolation density n=6 are retained. New anchor specifications and human-refinement explanations document the existing method.

E1.justification: Sections C.7–C.8 extend retained tasks to additional insertion objects, including brushes, syringes, and toothbrushes, and to clutter with similar distractors, occlusion, and language-based target disambiguation. The ten-task suite and two robotic platforms remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The tabulated comparator sets remain unchanged, including Mechanisms, MAGIC, Robot-ABC, ReKep, ReKep+, and the existing component replacements. However, new Appendix B.1 asserts experimental observations of unstable yaw from 6D pose estimators without identifying which estimators were tested or describing their comparison protocol. An additional comparator evaluation cannot be verified.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Tables 1–2 change the reported evaluation size from 20 to 25 trials per setting. New Table 7 introduces a localized protocol: sweep n=3–8 on four humanoid-platform tasks, stop after initial grasping, and exclude added dynamic interference. Existing full-task evaluations remain.

E4.justification: Sections C.7–C.9 substantially extend the supplementary analyses by testing anchor robustness across different object geometries, language grounding in cluttered and occluded scenes, and sensitivity to interpolation density. The earlier component ablations, lighting tests, interference-frequency analysis, and error breakdown are retained.

E5.justification: The reported number of robot trials per main-experiment setting increases from 20 to 25; retained appendix comparisons still use 20. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based uncertainty estimates, and the new ablation follows the existing success-count reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the 20-trial results with 25-trial results while retaining VLBiMan's overall lead; for example, its same-object, no-interference average in Table 1 changes from 85.0% to 85.3%. This is not a matched-setting performance gain. Figures 14–16 add successful object-generalization and clutter cases, while Table 7 adds pre-grasp results across six interpolation densities. Table 3 and the renumbered lighting and transfer tables retain their values.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Equations 1–7, and orientation-estimation algorithm are unchanged. The added discussions and density experiment introduce no new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about one-shot manipulation without retraining, compositional generalization, robustness, and cross-embodiment transfer. The additional appendix evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section C.6 clarifies the claimed one-time, limited burden of human refinement and newly identifies fully automatic segmentation as unresolved. Sections B.1 and C.7–C.9 expand explanations of lightweight anchors, clutter tolerance, and interpolation effects. The original hardware, deformability, and recovery limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Table 4 specifies objects, anchor types, and orientation-estimation requirements across the ten tasks. Section C.6 adds concrete refinement examples and explains when human intervention occurs. Hardware, demonstration collection, the default n=6, and access information are retained.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Appendix B.1 and C.7 expand positioning against the already cited SAM-6D and FoundationPose approaches, emphasizing model requirements and pose instability. Section C.8 additionally claims limited prior exploration of the illustrated clutter and occlusion challenges.

P1.justification: v3 makes a small title-word-order change, updates the publication header, adds acknowledgments, and expands the appendix introduction and explanatory subsections. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with three new multipanel rollout figures, Figures 14–16, and two new tables covering anchor specifications and interpolation density. Existing appendix Tables 4–5 become Tables 5–6, and several retained figures and tables are relocated or resized, including Table 1.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, Table 4 and Section C.6 clarify task-specific implementation choices and human intervention, while C.7–C.9 provide useful additional checks of generalization and the default interpolation density. These gains are qualified by qualitative-only clutter evidence and new reporting problems: Table 7's n=7 and n=8 same-object averages disagree with their counts, and C.9 claims disturbance benefits although that experiment excludes added interference. The additions modestly improve assessability and empirical support without resolving these weaknesses.
